a: Cities manage sewage and waste on a massive scale through integrated systems of collection, treatment, and disposal. Sewage management begins with a network of underground pipes that collect wastewater from homes, businesses, and industries. This wastewater flows to treatment plants, where it undergoes primary treatment (removal of large solids and settling), secondary treatment (biological processes using bacteria to break down organic matter), and tertiary treatment (filtration and disinfection). Advanced treatment plants also remove pharmaceuticals, microplastics, and other emerging contaminants. The treated water is then discharged into rivers, lakes, or oceans, or reused for irrigation and industrial purposes. Modern cities like Singapore have implemented NEWater programs that purify wastewater to drinking water standards. Waste management involves collecting, sorting, and processing municipal solid waste through a combination of curbside collection, transfer stations, and disposal facilities. Recycling programs separate paper, plastic, glass, and metal for reprocessing, while organic waste may be composted or converted to biogas through anaerobic digestion. Landfills are engineered with liners and leachate collection systems to prevent contamination of groundwater. Some cities, like San Francisco, have implemented mandatory composting and recycling programs that divert over 80% of waste from landfills. Waste-to-energy plants burn non-recyclable waste to generate electricity, reducing both waste volume and fossil fuel dependence. Smart city technologies are increasingly used to optimize collection routes, monitor fill levels in bins, and track waste streams in real time. Cities also manage hazardous waste separately, with special collection events and dedicated facilities for items like batteries, electronics, and chemicals. Stormwater management is another critical component — cities use green infrastructure like rain gardens, permeable pavements, and constructed wetlands to manage runoff and prevent combined sewer overflows during heavy rain.
